title: Subject-verb agreement
content: A singular third-person subject normally takes a singular verb in the present. He works, she has, and it is.

title: Third-person present simple
content: With he, she, or it, add -s or -es to most present-simple verbs. Study becomes studies and watch becomes watches.

title: Past simple with finished time
content: Use the past simple for a finished event at a finished time, such as yesterday, last week, or two days ago.

title: Present perfect form
content: Use have or has plus a past participle. Common irregular forms include gone, eaten, seen, and done.

title: Indefinite articles
content: Use a or an before a singular countable noun when it is not specific. Use an before a vowel sound, as in an engineer.

title: Many and much
content: Use many with plural countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns: many apples, much water.

title: Common preposition combinations
content: Some adjectives and verbs select a conventional preposition: interested in, good at, depend on, and arrive at/in.

title: Verb patterns
content: Enjoy, avoid, and finish are followed by a gerund. Want, need, and hope are commonly followed by to plus the base verb.

title: Modal plus base verb
content: A modal such as can, should, or must is followed by the base form without to: can go, should ask, must leave.

title: Question word order
content: In most wh-questions, put the auxiliary or be before the subject: What are you doing? Where did she go?

title: Comparative adjectives
content: Do not combine more with an adjective that already has a comparative form. Say better, easier, or more useful.

title: Uncountable nouns
content: Advice, information, feedback, and equipment are normally uncountable in standard English and do not take a plural -s.
source: SpeakMate Grammar Notes: Countable and uncountable nouns

title: Because and so
content: Use because to give a reason or so to show a result, but not both in the same clause: Because I was tired, I went to bed early. / I was tired, so I went to bed early.

title: Although and but
content: Although already expresses contrast, so it is not combined with but in the same clause: Although it was raining, we still went out.

title: He and she
content: English pronouns must match the gender of the person: use she for a woman or girl and he for a man or boy, even though the Chinese words sound the same.

title: Plural countable nouns
content: A number or quantifier such as two, many, or several is followed by a plural countable noun: two books, many students.
source: SpeakMate Grammar Notes: Countable and uncountable nouns

title: Want to do
content: Verbs like want, need, hope, and plan are followed by to plus the base verb: I want to go home.

title: Very with verbs
content: Very modifies adjectives or adverbs, not verbs. Say I really like it or I like it very much, not I very like it.

title: There is and there are
content: The verb in there is / there are agrees with the noun that follows: There are many people in the park. There is a book on the table.
source: SpeakMate Grammar Notes: There is and there are

title: Prepositions of time
content: Use on with days (on Monday), in with parts of the day (in the morning), and at with night, noon, and midnight (at night).
source: SpeakMate Grammar Notes: Prepositions of time

title: First conditional
content: In a real conditional, the if-clause uses the present simple, not will: If it rains, we will stay home.

title: So and such
content: So comes before an adjective (so beautiful), while such a/an comes before an adjective plus noun (such a beautiful place).
source: SpeakMate Grammar Notes: So and such

title: A few and a little
content: A few goes with plural countable nouns (a few friends), and a little goes with uncountable nouns (a little water).

title: Present continuous form
content: The present continuous is be plus the -ing form: I am going, she is cooking. Do not drop the be verb.
